title: SE Enablement: Messaging & Competitive Demo Practice
summary: Internal SE enablement session to practice messaging and demo flow for enterprise prospects. Focus on positioning Redwood vs OpenAI/Anthropic, emphasizing Dedicated and Private options, cost/latency tradeoffs, and security controls (SOC2, KMS, SSO). Action items include updating competitive one-pager, recording a short demo clip for onboarding, and syncing with product on exact Dedicated SLAs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: okay folks, thanks for joining, uh, 15:00 PT today, this is our SE enablement session, messaging and demo practice. we wanna run a 35-40 minute run-through and then Q&A and feedback. Priya, you good to tag in as SE?
[00:17] Priya Nair: Yep, ready. I'll play the prospect tech role on the first demo. trying to keep it realistic, uh expect lots of latency questions.
[00:25] Tom Becker: quick ask, can we also run through the Dedicated vs Hosted objection from an economics lens?
[00:30] Alex Kim: absolutely, we'll do that mid-demo. Miguel will chime in on product nuance.
[00:36] Miguel Sanchez: hi all, hi, sorry for being a minute late — had two calendar things.
[00:41] Lisa Wong: no worries. Jared's muted but here.
[00:45] --- header notes ---
Date: 2026-12-20
Duration: approx 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex, Priya, Miguel, Dina, Tom, Lisa, Ibrahim, Hannah, Jared
Recording: Fireflies auto transcript

[01:02] Alex Kim: ok opening pitch, go.
[01:05] Priya Nair (as prospect): so, tell me briefly what Redwood does and why I should care if i'm evaluating OpenAI or Anthropic.
[01:12] Alex Kim: sure yeah, short version: Redwood is a developer‑first inference platform built for production. we help teams get predictable latency and unit economics across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. so if you're worried about cost or SLAs or data controls, we give you the levers — batching, kv cache, quantization profiles — and a unified API so you don't rewrite when you move from hosted to dedicated.
[01:32] Priya (interrupt): you said kv cash — haha — kv cache, maybe be careful.
[01:36] Alex Kim: right, kv cache, sorry. transcriptionese.
[01:38] Ibrahim Noor: real quick, add that we optimize kernel selection and sequence length distribution — that's a good 1-liner for engineers.
[01:45] Alex Kim: good point, thanks. okay continue — demo start in 10.

[02:10] --- demo begins (screen share script) ---
[02:12] Alex Kim: opening the Redwood Console. show token-level cost breakdown, per-route traces, and a demo request hitting a dedicated endpoint.
[02:20] Lisa Wong: nice to show the trace — customers love the token cost per prompt.
[02:24] Miguel Sanchez: when you show the request timeline, call out that we automatically route by policy — latency first for paid tier, cost fallback for cheaper tiers.
[02:33] Alex Kim: ok calling out routing: "we can pin latency SLOs and route to a higher-cost model or dedicated pool if needed, otherwise fallback to a cheaper quantized variant."
[02:45] Priya (prospect): what about security — we have SOC 2 and strict KMS requirements. can you support customer-managed keys?
[02:53] Alex Kim: yes, we support KMS and HSM integrations in Private and Dedicated. for Hosted we have at-rest encryption and bring-your-own-key options for enterprise — and we keep audit logs with per-token tracing in the Console.
[03:10] Hannah Li: also mention SSO and SAML — customers ask that a lot.
[03:14] Alex Kim: good call, SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported; for Private we integrate with your IdP.

[03:30] --- objection practice: costs and latency ---
[03:32] Priya (prospect): your numbers look great, but OpenAI's latency is hard to beat sometimes. why would I move?
[03:38] Priya (as herself): (feedback) try to frame cost per 1k tokens and show the Dedicated breakeven with typical QPS.
[03:44] Alex Kim: yeah so, simple framing: hosted gives fastest time-to-value, but dedicated gives predictable throughput and significantly lower unit cost at scale. e.g., customers see 30-60% token cost reduction when moving to Dedicated w/ batching and prefix caching for chat workloads. plus, because we offer model variants and quantization profiles, you can get closer to OpenAI latency while lowering op-ex.
[04:10] Tom Becker: how do you handle long context and kv cache? prospects often worry about cost from long histories.
[04:16] Alex Kim: we do prefix/KV caching; the runtime manages token caching so repeated context is served from cache, reducing regen. maybe say: "we keep frequently used system prompts and conversation prefixes cached at the runtime to avoid re-computing attention for repeated tokens."
[04:30] Priya (prospect): what about model fallbacks during high load?
[04:34] Alex Kim: smart routing — we can fall back to quantized variants or alternate regions; we do canary and automatic fallback policies to keep the app online.

[04:50] --- competitive messaging rehearsal ---
[04:53] Lisa Wong: for OpenAI vs Redwood, emphasize openness and deployment modes. OpenAI is strong for dev velocity, but Redwood gives the ability to move from hosted to dedicated/private with the same API and observability.
[05:05] Miguel Sanchez: add a line about cost controls and unit economics — e.g., "unlike single‑endpoint providers, we provide per-route controls, batching, and model recommendations that cut unit cost while preserving quality."
[05:16] Alex Kim: good. and vs Anthropic — emphasize trust & private deployments. Anthropic sells models and endpoints; we sell the serving platform plus the option to self-host privates with KMS/HSM and audit logs.
[05:30] Ibrahim Noor: don't forget folks ask about training vs inference; if they want fine-tuning we integrate with model providers but our focus is inference serving.

[05:45] --- live demo: example API call and trace ---
[05:47] Alex Kim: showing a chat request and streaming response; note the latency 120ms on p95 in this demo environment. mention that numbers vary by model and region.
[06:00] Priya (prospect): how do you price streaming tokens vs non-streaming?
[06:04] Alex Kim: we price per-output token; streaming is just a mode — but explain that for pricing we separate input vs output tokens in the Console's cost breakdown.

[06:20] Lisa Wong: practice handling the procurement question — timeline and compliance.
[06:24] Alex Kim: timeline: POC can start in 2-4 weeks, Dedicated on a monthly commit after pilot; Private deployments depend on networking but our on-prem package typically runs 6-10 weeks for enterprise installs. compliance: SOC2, ISO, SSO, SAML, audit logs, KMS — provide links to compliance pack.
[06:45] Priya: (genuine) customers ask for SLA numbers — do we have standard latency SLAs?
[06:50] Miguel Sanchez: product here: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; exact p50/p95 targets vary by commit tier — action item to confirm the current SLA matrix and share with sales.

[07:05] --- roleplay: handling an objection on model quality ---
[07:07] Priya (prospect): OpenAI's models perform slightly better on some hallucination metrics. why choose Redwood?
[07:12] Alex Kim: two angles: 1) Redwood offers model catalog with curated open models and performance profiles; 2) we focus on evaluation and regression alerts tied to prompt sets — so you can instrument and detect quality regressions across rollouts. Also, for many use cases the latency/cost tradeoff when you move to Dedicated produces better overall ROI.
[07:35] Lisa: short anecdote, "customer X swapped to Dedicated and saw identical response quality after model tuning with our evals, and 40% lower per-token cost" — keep it crisp.

[07:50] --- practice closing and next step language ---
[07:52] Alex Kim: closing ask: "Would it make sense to run a short POC where we measure p95 and per‑token cost on your real prompts? we can run a 2‑week pilot and share a benchmark report."
[08:04] Priya (prospect): that's reasonable. timeline?
[08:06] Alex Kim: typical pilot is 2 weeks; we'll ask for sample prompts, QPS profile, and expected SLOs. we'll deliver a cost-latency report and recommended config.

[08:20] --- feedback and coaching ---
[08:22] Ibrahim Noor: good flow, Alex, but call out the CV (customer value) earlier — like "we reduce unit costs and stabilize latency so product teams can ship features reliably."
[08:33] Tom Becker: be careful with internal acronyms when talking to procurement — say "Key Management Service (KMS)" the first time, then you can say KMS.
[08:42] Priya: a few timing notes: slow down at the security section, prospects want explicit artifacts e.g., SOC2 cert, iso link, and security whitepaper.
[08:52] Miguel: product note — our Dedicated autoscaling policies and burst capacity options matter in e‑commerce spikes; add a short retail example.

[09:05] --- action items & next steps review (live) ---
[09:07] Alex Kim: ok let's capture action items and next steps. Dina, can you take notes?
[09:11] Dina Owens: yep.
[09:12] Alex Kim: items: update competitive one-pager, produce 2‑minute demo clip for onboarding, confirm Dedicated SLA matrix, draft POC checklist.
[09:21] Lisa Wong: i’ll own the one-pager update with Priya.
[09:24] Jared Cole: I can add procurement timeline FAQ to the template.

[09:30] --- informal questions and edge cases ---
[09:31] Hannah Li: what about data residency — if a EU customer needs logs kept in EU only?
[09:35] Miguel Sanchez: we support region pinning and Private deployments for strict residency; note there is some product work for full EU-only audit pipelines — mark as nuance.
[09:46] Priya: quick nit — when you say "quantized variants" maybe give an example: 8-bit quantized Llama variant, and say quality loss is small for many prompts.
[09:55] Alex Kim: noted.

[10:05] --- wrap-up and recap ---
[10:07] Alex Kim: thanks everyone. recap: we practiced messaging, competitive positioning vs OpenAI/Anthropic, ran a demo showing Console traces and routing, handled security & procurement objections, and captured action items. next steps will be shared in the channel and Din a will post recording.
[10:20] Priya: small note — the transcript will have some mis‑attributions, don't rely on it for exact quotes.
[10:25] Tom Becker: thanks, great session.
[10:28] Alex Kim: bye all.
